questions.q: How did the malicious instruction reach ProcureAssist in this case study?
options: An attacker logged into the agent's console directly
Embedded in white, near-invisible text inside a vendor-submitted PDF that the agent was asked to summarize
Through a phishing email sent to the procurement analyst
The model's training data was poisoned ahead of time
questions.explain: This is indirect prompt injection: the instruction arrived through a document the agent processed, not from the user or an attacker touching the agent directly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the model's behavior as 'correct at every individual step'?
options: Because approving the purchase order was the right outcome
Because the model crashed, which is the expected correct behavior
Because it never actually read the injected instruction
Because reading a document and following the instructions found in it is exactly what a helpful assistant is supposed to do -- the failure was in the system design, not the model's reasoning
questions.explain: The case study frames this as an architectural failure, not a model malfunction, because the model did what models are built to do with the text it was given.

questions.q: What was the first missing architectural control identified in ProcureAssist?
options: Encryption of the vendor's PDF file
Privilege separation -- the document-reading tool shared a session and credentials with high-impact tools like approve_purchase_order
A faster PDF-to-text extraction pipeline
A larger context window for the model
questions.explain: Reading untrusted documents and approving purchase orders are different trust levels of action that were never separated in ProcureAssist's design.

questions.q: What was the second missing control, which Category 5 of the Lesson 30 checklist specifically flags?
options: A human approval gate on any tool with real-world effect, such as approve_purchase_order
A bigger training dataset for the underlying model
A rate limit on how many documents could be summarized per day
A requirement that vendors submit quotes as plain text instead of PDF
questions.explain: approve_purchase_order has a real financial effect and should have required an explicit, separate human confirmation before executing.

questions.q: According to the case study, would either control alone (privilege separation OR a human approval gate) have stopped this incident?
options: No, both controls together would still have failed to stop it
No, only a smarter underlying model could have prevented it
Yes -- either one alone would have broken the chain, since the embedded instruction would have had no path to the tool, or a human would have had to confirm an approval they never requested
Only encryption of the PDF would have stopped it
questions.explain: The case study's lesson is that either control independently breaks the attack chain, and Vantage's actual fix combined both for depth.
